structure.title: I
structure.summary: In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg and rents a modest bungalow between two grand estates; after feeling lonely, he gains a sense of belonging when a stranger asks him for directions to West Egg village. He drives by car to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, a domineering Yale alumnus, at their lavish Georgian Colonial mansion overlooking the bay, where he is introduced to Jordan Baker, an aloof young woman. During dinner, Tom passionately defends white supremacy using 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires,' while Daisy and Jordan respond with detached irony; a telephone call from Tom’s mistress in New York interrupts the meal, which Jordan confirms to Nick in confidence. Daisy, in a moment of vulnerability, tells Nick she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool,' revealing her disillusionment with societal expectations. Later, as Nick prepares to leave, Daisy and Tom tease him about a rumored engagement to a woman out West, which he denies. Returning to West Egg, Nick stops his car and sits on an abandoned grass roller in his yard, where he observes Mr. Gatsby standing alone on the lawn, stretching his arms toward the dark water and trembling as he gazes at a distant green light before vanishing into the shadows.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, forced to disembark at the desolate Valley of Ashes, where they walk under the faded, gigantic eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg to George B. Wilson’s run-down garage; there, Myrtle Wilson emerges—vibrant yet unattractive—and dismissively ignores her pale, spiritless husband as she and Tom arrange to meet in New York, with Nick reluctantly accompanying them. They take a lavender taxicab to a rented top-floor apartment at 158th Street, where Myrtle impulsively buys a puppy she mistakes for a police dog, summons her sister Catherine and the McKees, and transforms into a performative, drunken persona in a cream chiffon dress, shouting exaggerated stories about her affair with Tom and mocking her husband while the apartment fills with oversized furniture and an enlarged photograph of her mother; the evening descends into chaos when Myrtle, inebriated, repeatedly invokes Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose, after which women scramble for towels, blood stains the bathroom floor and a copy of Town Tattle, and Nick departs with the dazed Mr. McKee before finding himself alone at Pennsylvania Station at dawn, exhausted and cold after witnessing the collapse of the evening’s illusions.

structure.title: III
characters_present: the drunk man in the library
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway receiving a formal invitation to attend one of Jay Gatsby’s extravagant Saturday evening parties at his West Egg mansion, where guests arrive by car and train amid orchestras, five crates of weekly fruit deliveries, and bars stocked with forgotten cordials. Amid wild rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy, Nick Carraway encounters eccentric figures including a drunken man in the library who verifies the authenticity of Gatsby’s unread books, and later meets Jordan Baker and a war veteran who offers him a ride in a newly purchased hydroplane—yet Gatsby remains unseen until Nick Carraway, after consuming champagne, is introduced to him by name, revealing a surprising youth and composure; Gatsby invites Nick Carraway to fly in his hydroplane the next morning, while Jordan expresses skepticism about his claim of attending Oxford. As the party descends into chaos—champagne-fueled tears, marital fights, and a woman falling asleep mid-song—Nick Carraway observes Gatsby standing apart, sober and detached, before Jordan is summoned alone to speak with him for an hour. The evening ends with a car crash on Gatsby’s drive: a new coupé loses a wheel after hitting a wall, leaving Owl Eyes and another disoriented man in the wreckage, with the passenger insisting he wasn’t driving and asking where to find a gas station, as Nick Carraway departs to find Gatsby standing alone on the porch, formally bidding farewell under a faint moon. In a reflective interlude, Nick Carraway describes his daily routine in New York: walking to work at the Probity Trust, dining with clerks in crowded restaurants, and studying investments at the Yale Club, while romanticizing strangers on Fifth Avenue at twilight and feeling a haunting loneliness among young clerks; he reconnects with Jordan Baker, discovering her dishonesty through her lie about damaging a borrowed car and her past cheating in a golf tournament, and though unsettled by her reckless attitude toward driving—asserting others must avoid her—he remains drawn to her while still writing weekly letters signed 'Love, Nick' to a woman back home.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion hosts a chaotic, extravagant party attended by dozens of guests arriving by car from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, including the Chester Beckers, Leeches, Blackbucks, Snells, Dancies, Gus Waize, Francis Bull, and a prince referred to as 'Duke,' while some guests engage in reckless behavior such as Clarence Endive’s fight with a bum and Ripley Snell being run over by Mrs. Ulysses Swett’s car; later, on a late July morning, Gatsby picks up Nick Carraway in his cream-colored car with nickel trim to drive to New York, where he delivers an elaborate, seemingly rehearsed account of his life—claiming Oxford education, European aristocratic travels, and wartime heroism in the Argonne Forest, backed by a Montenegrin medal and an Oxford photograph—and reveals he intends to make a request through Jordan Baker, later using a white card to evade a police stop; at noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a grotesque gambler with human-molar cuff buttons who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and confesses to fixing the 1919 World Series, before Gatsby abruptly leaves to make a phone call and vanishes when Nick Carraway attempts to introduce him to Tom Buchanan; in a flashback to October 1917, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby in Louisville, witnessing their romantic gaze, and later learning of Daisy’s lavish wedding to Tom Buchanan, her drunken distress on the eve of marriage clutching a letter, and her subsequent scandalous affair and relocation to Chicago; after leaving the Plaza Hotel at twilight, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be across the bay from Daisy and asks him to invite Daisy for tea so Gatsby can visit unannounced, fearing to offend Nick Carraway or trust Jordan directly, as he wants Daisy to see his house through Nick Carraway’s home—leading Nick Carraway to shift focus to Jordan, drawing her close as they ride through Central Park and reflecting on the divisions among the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, and the tired.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy night at West Egg, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit with no party in progress, only wind causing the lights to flicker; Gatsby approaches him nervously, revealing his plan to reunite with Daisy through Nick and subtly offering him a side business opportunity, which Nick declines. The next morning, rain prompts Gatsby to send a man to cut Nick’s lawn, and he arrives in a white flannel suit, silver shirt, and gold tie, visibly shaken as Daisy arrives by large open car with chauffeur Ferdie; Gatsby freezes upon seeing her, nearly knocking over a clock, but after a long silence, they reconnect emotionally, with Daisy in tears, and Gatsby transforms into a radiant figure who invites her to tour his mansion. Inside the opulent estate, they pass through Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons, encountering Mr. Klipspringer in pajamas, and Gatsby overwhelms Daisy by throwing his collection of expensive shirts—coral, apple-green, lavender, and indigo-blue with monograms—onto the table, causing her to sob uncontrollably at their beauty. As the rain stops and sunlight enters, Gatsby points out the diminished green light at Daisy’s dock, and Nick Carraway examines photographs of Dan Cody and a youthful Gatsby in yachting attire; Gatsby abruptly ends a phone call about Detroit being an unsuitable 'small town', and as pink and golden clouds form over the Sound, Daisy poetically wishes to put Gatsby inside them. He summons Klipspringer to play piano poorly in the music room, lights Daisy’s cigarette, and sits with her in near-darkness as Nick departs, leaving them absorbed in each other, Gatsby’s face flickering with doubt before he is reclaimed by Daisy’s voice, described as a 'deathless song'.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s West Egg mansion seeking a statement based on unconfirmed rumors of underground schemes, unaware that Gatsby’s true identity is James Gatz of North Dakota, who at seventeen changed his name after encountering Dan Cody’s yacht anchored in Little Girl Bay on Lake Superior; Gatz boarded the yacht and served as Cody’s protégé for five years in multiple roles, absorbing the ways of wealth before losing a $25,000 inheritance to Ella Kaye after Cody’s death, yet clung fiercely to his self-invented persona, living in constant reverie of an idealized version of himself. Weeks later, Nick visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive unexpectedly on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous and eager to please, insists on offering them drinks despite their cold indifference, revealing his anxiety over Tom’s presence. Later, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is overwhelmed by the vulgarity of West Egg and emotionally distant, while Tom openly mocks the guests and suspects Gatsby is a bootlegger; after the party ends, Gatsby confides in Nick that Daisy did not enjoy the evening and insists he must make her admit she never loved Tom so they can return to Louisville and recreate their past, rooted in a moonlit kiss five years earlier that he believes still holds the power to restore everything.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On a broiling summer afternoon, Nick arrives at the Buchanans’ house by train to find Gatsby waiting; the mansion is unnervingly quiet after Gatsby replaced his servants with Wolfsheim’s reclusive relatives. Daisy kisses Gatsby and declares her love in front of Tom, who reacts with stunned realization as he argues on the telephone. The group departs for town in two cars—Tom insists on driving Gatsby’s yellow coupé while Gatsby rides in Tom’s coupe with Nick and Jordan, revealing growing hostility. During the drive, Tom mocks Gatsby’s Oxford claim and probes his past, leading them to stop at Wilson’s garage in the Valley of Ashes, where a sick and emotionally broken Wilson reveals he plans to leave with Myrtle and wants to buy Tom’s old car; Tom, unaware Wilson has discovered Myrtle’s infidelity, declares he will take her away, while Myrtle watches from the window, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife in jealous terror. The group continues to the Plaza Hotel, where Tom aggressively exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties to Meyer Wolfsheim and shatters his image; Daisy, overwhelmed, admits she once loved Tom but now loves Gatsby—only to retract and confess she loved both, collapsing emotionally. Tom forces Daisy and Gatsby to leave together in Gatsby’s car, while Nick and Jordan depart separately. Later, Michaelis discovers George Wilson severely ill in his garage office, where Wilson calmly reveals he has locked Myrtle upstairs and plans to leave in two days; when Michaelis returns shortly after seven, he witnesses Myrtle rushing out and being struck by a speeding yellow car that flees the scene, leaving her dead with a crushed left breast and torn shirtwaist. Tom and Nick arrive at the garage to find Myrtle’s body and a crowd gathered; Wilson hysterically cries 'Oh, my Ga-od!' as witnesses identify the fleeing vehicle as a large yellow car. Tom denies driving it, claims his own car is blue, and is corroborated by others, then carries Wilson into the office before driving away in tears, calling the driver a 'God damned coward.' Finally, Nick, feeling sick and disillusioned after leaving the Buchanans’, encounters Gatsby emerging from the shrubbery, who reveals he has waited all night to protect Daisy, confessing she was driving the car that killed Myrtle and that he intends to take the blame; Nick secretly observes Tom and Daisy calmly eating cold chicken and drinking ale together in the kitchen, silently reconciled, before leaving Gatsby alone in the moonlight, vigilantly watching a house where his dream has already collapsed.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway finds Gatsby dejected in his mansion’s hallway after waiting all night for Daisy to appear at her window—she briefly lit a light before turning it off. They wander the dusty, musty rooms searching for cigarettes, and Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal to evade suspicion over Daisy’s car, but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the hope that she will choose him. In a vulnerable confession, Gatsby recounts his youthful romance with Daisy, admitting he deceived her into believing he was wealthy and socially equivalent, and became irrevocably bound to her as if married. Later, he reflects on returning to Louisville after the war, penniless, walking the streets where they once loved, feeling he had left her behind as the train pulled away. At two o’clock, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, instructs the butler to bring any call to the pool, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage (which guests had once used), and orders the damaged open car not be driven; he walks alone toward the pool. No call arrives, and at some point, gunshots are heard. Nick Carraway rushes to the house, and the staff discovers Gatsby’s body floating on the mattress in the pool, while the gardener later finds George Wilson’s body in the grass—Wilson, having learned Gatsby’s name by asking for directions, had come seeking justice for Myrtle’s death. The chapter ends with the tragic convergence of their fates.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, his mansion is overrun by police, photographers, and curious onlookers, while media reports falsely label Wilson a 'madman' and Catherine denies any connection between Gatsby and Myrtle, leading authorities to close the case as grief-driven madness. Nick Carraway, overwhelmed by Gatsby’s isolation, attempts in vain to contact Daisy and Meyer Wolfsheim, receiving only a cold, evasive letter from Wolfsheim citing business obligations; a mistaken long-distance call from Chicago ends in stunned silence after Nick Carraway delivers the news of Gatsby’s death. On the third day, Henry C. Gatz arrives by train from Minnesota, frail and bundled in a cheap ulster, and is shown Gatsby’s body and mansion, where his grief transforms into awed pride as he displays a childhood notebook detailing Gatsby’s self-improvement schedule. Despite Nick Carraway’s efforts, nearly all guests refuse to attend the funeral—Klipspringer calls only to request his tennis shoes, and Wolfsheim declines, citing a personal rule against involvement after death. At the 3 p.m. funeral, only Gatz, the Lutheran minister from Flushing, Nick Carraway, and the servants are present as rain falls; an unexpected figure, the man with owl-eyed glasses, arrives splashing through the mud, wipes rain from his glasses to view Gatsby’s grave, murmurs 'Amen to that' in response to 'Blessed are the dead that the rain falls on,' and quietly calls Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Later, Nick Carraway encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson that Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary given Wilson’s aggression, and Nick Carraway, repulsed yet detached, shakes his hand. After packing and selling his car, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s abandoned house at night, erases an obscene word scrawled on the steps, and walks to the beach, where he reflects on Gatsby’s futile pursuit of the green light and the enduring human struggle against a current that pushes us back into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Henry C. Gatz recounts his arrival in West Egg and his introduction to the glittering yet hollow world of Long Island’s elite through his neighbor, the enigmatic Jay Gatsby. He is drawn into the orbit of Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whose wealth masks deep moral decay, and meets Jordan Baker, a detached and dishonest golfer who becomes his reluctant companion. Through Jordan, Gatz learns that Gatsby’s lavish parties and mysterious persona are all orchestrated to rekindle a long-lost romance with Daisy, whom he met five years earlier as a poor officer named James Gatz. Gatsby, once a dreamer from North Dakota, reinvented himself entirely—adopting wealth, status, and an Oxford pedigree—to win back the woman who had married Tom while he was away at war. Gatz becomes the reluctant intermediary in Gatsby’s plan to reunite with Daisy, hosting their fateful tea, where old feelings resurface amid the opulence of Gatsby’s mansion.

As summer turns to heat, tensions escalate when Tom Buchanan confronts Gatsby at the Plaza Hotel, exposing his criminal ties to Meyer Wolfsheim and shattering his illusion of legitimacy. Daisy, overwhelmed, admits she once loved both men but ultimately retreats into the safety of her marriage, leaving Gatsby shattered. The turning point arrives when Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, is killed by a speeding yellow car—driven by Daisy but owned by Gatsby. Tom, in a cruel act of betrayal, tells George Wilson that Gatsby was the driver, inciting Wilson’s vengeful pursuit. Meanwhile, Gatsby, still clinging to the belief that Daisy will choose him, waits vigilantly outside her house, taking blame for the accident to protect her. His dream, already frayed by her indifference and the vulgarity of his own world, collapses as he remains alone in the moonlight, watching a house where his idealized past has already died.

After Gatsby’s murder at the hands of the grieving Wilson, Henry C. Gatz is left to navigate the hollow aftermath: no one attends the funeral except Gatsby’s father, who arrives with a childhood notebook revealing the boy’s relentless self-improvement and quiet ambition. Gatz is stunned by the depth of Gatsby’s longing and the emptiness of his legacy—guests vanish, Wolfsheim refuses involvement, and even Klipspringer only calls to retrieve his tennis shoes. As Gatz reflects on the scene, he sees Gatsby not as a fraud but as a tragic idealist who believed in the green light across the bay—the unattainable dream of renewal, love, and self-reinvention. In the final moments, standing on the beach where Gatsby once reached toward that distant glow, Gatz observes how all people are pushed back by time and circumstance, yet still yearn forward, forever caught between the past they cherish and the future they can never reclaim.
